title: About
text:
I use this website as a public mathematical notebook. The main purpose is not to make finished survey articles, but to record ideas clearly enough that they remain useful months later.
The guiding style is simple: state the result, explain the geometric picture, then write the proof in a form that can be checked.

title: Home
text:

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 3
text:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(x_0\in\Omega\).
Define the Dirac delta at \(x_0\) by
\[
\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)
=
\varphi(x_0),
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).
\]
Prove that \(\delta_{x_0}\) is a distribution on \(\Omega\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 3
text:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(x_0\in\Omega\).
Define the Dirac delta at \(x_0\) by
\[
\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)
=
\varphi(x_0),
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).
\]
Prove that \(\delta_{x_0}\) is a distribution on \(\Omega\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 3
text:
Solution
Recall that a distribution on \(\Omega\) is a continuous linear functional on the space of test functions
\[
\mathcal D(\Omega)
=
C_c^\infty(\Omega).
\]
Thus we need to prove that
\[
\delta_{x_0}:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb R
\]
is linear and continuous.

Linearity
Let \(\varphi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)\) and let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{x_0}(a\varphi+b\psi)
&=
(a\varphi+b\psi)(x_0)\\
&=
a\varphi(x_0)+b\psi(x_0)\\
&=
a\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)
+
b\delta_{x_0}(\psi).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \(\delta_{x_0}\) is linear.


Continuity
Let \(K\subset\Omega\) be compact. For every
\[
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)
\]
with
\[
\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset K,
\]
we have
\[
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)|
=
|\varphi(x_0)|.
\]
If \(x_0\notin K\), then
\[
\varphi(x_0)=0,
\]
and hence
\[
\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)=0.
\]
If \(x_0\in K\), then
\[
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)|
=
|\varphi(x_0)|
\leq
\sup_{x\in K}|\varphi(x)|.
\]
Therefore, in either case,
\[
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)|
\leq
\sup_{x\in K}|\varphi(x)|.
\]
The right-hand side is one of the standard seminorms defining the topology of
\[
C_c^\infty(\Omega).
\]
Hence \(\delta_{x_0}\) is continuous.
Equivalently, suppose that
\[
\varphi_j\to0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D(\Omega).
\]
Then there exists a compact set
\[
K\subset\Omega
\]
such that
\[
\operatorname{supp}\varphi_j\subset K
\]
for all sufficiently large \(j\), and
\[
\sup_{x\in K}
|D^\alpha\varphi_j(x)|
\to0
\]
for every multi-index \(\alpha\).
Taking \(\alpha=0\), we obtain
\[
\sup_{x\in K}|\varphi_j(x)|
\to0.
\]
Hence
\[
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi_j)|
=
|\varphi_j(x_0)|
\leq
\sup_{x\in K}|\varphi_j(x)|
\to0.
\]
Therefore \(\delta_{x_0}\) is continuous on \(\mathcal D(\Omega)\).
We conclude that
\[
\boxed{
\delta_{x_0}\in\mathcal D'(\Omega).
}
\]
Thus the Dirac delta is a distribution.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 3
text:
Remark
The Dirac delta is a distribution of order zero, since
\[
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)|
\leq
\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}.
\]
It is not induced by any locally integrable function.
Indeed, if there were some
\[
f\in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega)
\]
such that
\[
\varphi(x_0)
=
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx
\]
for every \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)\), then testing against functions supported away from \(x_0\) would imply
\[
f=0
\]
almost everywhere on
\[
\Omega\setminus\{x_0\}.
\]
Since the singleton \(\{x_0\}\) has Lebesgue measure zero, this would imply
\[
f=0
\]
almost everywhere in \(\Omega\), contradicting
\[
\delta_{x_0}\neq0.
\]
Thus the Dirac delta is a genuine distribution rather than an ordinary function.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 2, Problem 2
text:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(X'\) denote its dual space.

Prove that \(X\) is reflexive if and only if \(X'\) is reflexive.
Prove that if \(X'\) is separable, then \(X\) is separable.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 2, Problem 2
text:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(X'\) denote its dual space.

Prove that \(X\) is reflexive if and only if \(X'\) is reflexive.
Prove that if \(X'\) is separable, then \(X\) is separable.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 2, Problem 2
text:
Solution

1. Reflexivity of \(X\) and \(X'\)
Recall the canonical embedding
\[
J_X:X\longrightarrow X'',
\qquad
J_X(x)(f)=f(x),
\]
for \(x\in X\) and \(f\in X'\).
The space \(X\) is reflexive precisely when \(J_X\) is surjective.
We prove the two implications separately.

\(X\) reflexive implies \(X'\) reflexive
Suppose that \(X\) is reflexive. Then
\[
J_X(X)=X''.
\]
We want to show that the canonical embedding
\[
J_{X'}:X'\longrightarrow X'''
\]
is surjective.
Let
\[
F\in X'''.
\]
Define \(f:X\to\mathbb K\) by
\[
f(x)=F(J_Xx),
\]
where \(\mathbb K=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\).
Since \(F\) and \(J_X\) are bounded linear maps, \(f\in X'\).
We claim that
\[
F=J_{X'}f.
\]
Indeed, let \(x''\in X''\). Since \(X\) is reflexive, there exists \(x\in X\) such that
\[
x''=J_Xx.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(J_{X'}f)(x'')
&=x''(f)\\
&=(J_Xx)(f)\\
&=f(x)\\
&=F(J_Xx)\\
&=F(x'').
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
F=J_{X'}f.
\]
Hence \(J_{X'}\) is surjective, and therefore \(X'\) is reflexive.


\(X'\) reflexive implies \(X\) reflexive
Now suppose that \(X'\) is reflexive.
Assume, toward a contradiction, that \(X\) is not reflexive. Then
\[
J_X(X)\subsetneq X''.
\]
Since \(J_X\) is an isometry and \(X\) is Banach, \(J_X(X)\) is a closed subspace of \(X''\).
By the Hahn–Banach theorem, there exists a nonzero functional
\[
F\in X'''
\]
such that
\[
F|_{J_X(X)}=0.
\]
Since \(X'\) is reflexive, the canonical map
\[
J_{X'}:X'\to X'''
\]
is surjective. Hence there exists \(f\in X'\) such that
\[
F=J_{X'}f.
\]
For every \(x\in X\),
\[
0
=
F(J_Xx)
=
(J_{X'}f)(J_Xx).
\]
But
\[
(J_{X'}f)(J_Xx)
=
(J_Xx)(f)
=
f(x).
\]
Therefore,
\[
f(x)=0
\]
for every \(x\in X\), so \(f=0\). Consequently,
\[
F=J_{X'}f=0,
\]
contradicting the choice of \(F\).
Thus \(J_X(X)=X''\), and hence \(X\) is reflexive.
We have proved
\[
\boxed{
X\text{ is reflexive}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X'\text{ is reflexive}.
}
\]



2. Separability of \(X'\) implies separability of \(X\)
Suppose that \(X'\) is separable.
If \(X=\{0\}\), the conclusion is trivial, so assume \(X\neq\{0\}\).
Since \(X'\) is separable, its unit sphere
\[
S_{X'}
=
\{f\in X':\|f\|=1\}
\]
contains a countable dense subset. Let
\[
\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty
\]
be dense in \(S_{X'}\).
For every \(n\), since
\[
\|f_n\|=1,
\]
by the definition of the operator norm we can choose \(x_n\in X\) such that
\[
\|x_n\|=1
\]
and
\[
|f_n(x_n)|>\frac12.
\]
Let
\[
M
=
\overline{\operatorname{span}\{x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}}.
\]
We claim that
\[
M=X.
\]
Suppose otherwise. Then \(M\) is a proper closed subspace of \(X\). By the Hahn–Banach theorem, there exists
\[
f\in X'
\]
such that
\[
\|f\|=1,
\qquad
f|_M=0.
\]
Since \(\{f_n\}\) is dense in \(S_{X'}\), there exists \(n\) such that
\[
\|f-f_n\|<\frac14.
\]
Since \(x_n\in M\), we have
\[
f(x_n)=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|f_n(x_n)|
&=
|(f_n-f)(x_n)|\\
&\leq
\|f_n-f\|\|x_n\|\\
&<
\frac14.
\end{aligned}
\]
This contradicts our choice of \(x_n\), for which
\[
|f_n(x_n)|>\frac12.
\]
Hence
\[
M=X.
\]
Therefore,
\[
X
=
\overline{\operatorname{span}\{x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}}.
\]
The linear span of a countable set is separable. Indeed, the finite linear combinations of the \(x_n\) with rational coefficients are countable and dense in the real case; in the complex case one may use coefficients in
\[
\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q.
\]
Consequently, \(X\) is separable.
Thus
\[
\boxed{
X'\text{ separable}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X\text{ separable}.
}
\]

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 2, Problem 2
text:
Remark
The converse of the second statement is false in general.
A Banach space may be separable while its dual is nonseparable. The standard example is
\[
X=\ell^1.
\]
The space \(\ell^1\) is separable, whereas
\[
(\ell^1)'=\ell^\infty
\]
is not separable.
Thus
\[
X'\text{ separable}
\Longrightarrow
X\text{ separable},
\]
but in general
\[
X\text{ separable}
\nRightarrow
X'\text{ separable}.
\]
However, if \(X\) is both separable and reflexive, then \(X'\) is also separable.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 1
text:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex open set and let
\[
f\in C^1(\Omega).
\]
Prove that for any \(x,y\in\Omega\), there exists a point
\[
\xi\in [x,y]
\]
such that
\[
f(y)-f(x)
=
\nabla f(\xi)\cdot (y-x).
\]
Here
\[
[x,y]
=
\{x+t(y-x):0\leq t\leq1\}
\]
denotes the line segment joining \(x\) and \(y\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 1
text:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex open set and let
\[
f\in C^1(\Omega).
\]
Prove that for any \(x,y\in\Omega\), there exists a point
\[
\xi\in [x,y]
\]
such that
\[
f(y)-f(x)
=
\nabla f(\xi)\cdot (y-x).
\]
Here
\[
[x,y]
=
\{x+t(y-x):0\leq t\leq1\}
\]
denotes the line segment joining \(x\) and \(y\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 1
text:
Solution
If \(x=y\), the conclusion is immediate. Thus assume that \(x\neq y\).
Since \(\Omega\) is convex,
\[
x+t(y-x)\in\Omega
\]
for every \(t\in[0,1]\).
Define the one-dimensional function
\[
g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R
\]
by
\[
g(t)
=
f\bigl(x+t(y-x)\bigr).
\]
Since \(f\in C^1(\Omega)\), we have
\[
g\in C^1([0,1]).
\]
By the ordinary one-dimensional Lagrange mean value theorem, there exists some
\[
t_0\in(0,1)
\]
such that
\[
g(1)-g(0)=g'(t_0).
\]
Now
\[
g(1)=f(y),
\qquad
g(0)=f(x).
\]
By the chain rule,
\[
g'(t)
=
\nabla f\bigl(x+t(y-x)\bigr)\cdot(y-x).
\]
Therefore,
\[
f(y)-f(x)
=
\nabla f\bigl(x+t_0(y-x)\bigr)\cdot(y-x).
\]
Set
\[
\xi=x+t_0(y-x).
\]
Then \(\xi\in[x,y]\), and hence
\[
\boxed{
f(y)-f(x)
=
\nabla f(\xi)\cdot(y-x).
}
\]
This proves the multivariable Lagrange mean value theorem.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 1
text:
Remark
The convexity assumption guarantees that the entire line segment joining \(x\) and \(y\) remains inside \(\Omega\). This allows the multidimensional problem to be reduced directly to the one-dimensional mean value theorem.
As an immediate consequence,
\[
|f(y)-f(x)|
\leq
\sup_{z\in[x,y]}|\nabla f(z)|\,|x-y|.
\]
In particular, if \(\Omega\) is convex and
\[
\|\nabla f\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}<\infty,
\]
then
\[
|f(y)-f(x)|
\leq
\|\nabla f\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}|x-y|,
\]
so \(f\) is Lipschitz continuous on \(\Omega\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 1
text:
For \(\sigma>0\), define the Gaussian function
\[
f_\sigma(x)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
\]
Let \(T_\sigma\) be the distribution induced by \(f_\sigma\):
\[
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{\mathbb R}f_\sigma(x)\varphi(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R).
\]
Prove that
\[
T_\sigma\longrightarrow\delta_0
\]
in the sense of distributions as \(\sigma\to0\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 1
text:
For \(\sigma>0\), define the Gaussian function
\[
f_\sigma(x)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
\]
Let \(T_\sigma\) be the distribution induced by \(f_\sigma\):
\[
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{\mathbb R}f_\sigma(x)\varphi(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R).
\]
Prove that
\[
T_\sigma\longrightarrow\delta_0
\]
in the sense of distributions as \(\sigma\to0\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 1
text:
Solution
Recall that
\[
T_\sigma\to\delta_0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)
\]
means that for every test function
\[
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R),
\]
we have
\[
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
\longrightarrow
\langle\delta_0,\varphi\rangle
=
\varphi(0).
\]
Let \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\). Then
\[
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}
\varphi(x)\,dx.
\]
Make the change of variables
\[
x=\sigma y.
\]
Then
\[
dx=\sigma\,dy,
\]
and hence
\[
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}
\varphi(\sigma y)\,dy.
\]
For every fixed \(y\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\varphi(\sigma y)\to\varphi(0)
\]
as \(\sigma\to0\).
Moreover,
\[
|\varphi(\sigma y)|
\leq
\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)},
\]
and therefore
\[
\left|
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}
\varphi(\sigma y)
\right|
\leq
\frac{\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}.
\]
The function on the right belongs to \(L^1(\mathbb R)\). Thus, by the dominated convergence theorem,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{\sigma\to0}
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
&=
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}
\varphi(0)\,dy\\
&=
\varphi(0)
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}\,dy.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since the Gaussian is normalized,
\[
\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
e^{-y^2/2}\,dy
=
1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\lim_{\sigma\to0}
\langle T_\sigma,\varphi\rangle
=
\varphi(0)
=
\langle\delta_0,\varphi\rangle.
\]
Since this holds for every test function \(\varphi\), we conclude that
\[
\boxed{
T_\sigma\longrightarrow\delta_0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R).
}
\]

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 1
text:
Remark
The family \(\{f_\sigma\}_{\sigma>0}\) is an example of an approximate identity. It satisfies
\[
f_\sigma\geq0,
\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}f_\sigma(x)\,dx=1,
\]
while its mass becomes increasingly concentrated near the origin as \(\sigma\to0\).
Thus the Dirac delta can be understood as the distributional limit of a family of smooth functions, even though \(\delta_0\) itself cannot be represented by a locally integrable function.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 3
text:
Let
\[
u(x)=|x|,
\qquad
x\in\mathbb R.
\]
Compute the second derivative of \(u\) in the sense of distributions.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 3
text:
Let
\[
u(x)=|x|,
\qquad
x\in\mathbb R.
\]
Compute the second derivative of \(u\) in the sense of distributions.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 3
text:
Solution
Since
\[
u(x)=|x|\in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\mathbb R),
\]
it defines a distribution on \(\mathbb R\).
We claim that
\[
\boxed{
u''=2\delta_0
}
\]
in the sense of distributions.
Let
\[
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R).
\]
By the definition of the second distributional derivative,
\[
\langle u'',\varphi\rangle
=
\langle u,\varphi''\rangle.
\]
Thus
\[
\langle u'',\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{\mathbb R}|x|\varphi''(x)\,dx.
\]
Split the integral at the origin:
\[
\langle u'',\varphi\rangle
=
\int_{-\infty}^0(-x)\varphi''(x)\,dx
+
\int_0^\infty x\varphi''(x)\,dx.
\]
For the first integral, integration by parts gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\infty}^0(-x)\varphi''(x)\,dx
&=
\left[(-x)\varphi'(x)\right]_{-\infty}^0
+
\int_{-\infty}^0\varphi'(x)\,dx\\
&=
\varphi(0).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the boundary term vanishes because \(\varphi\) has compact support.
Similarly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^\infty x\varphi''(x)\,dx
&=
\left[x\varphi'(x)\right]_0^\infty
-
\int_0^\infty\varphi'(x)\,dx\\
&=
\varphi(0).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\langle u'',\varphi\rangle
=
2\varphi(0).
\]
But
\[
\langle\delta_0,\varphi\rangle
=
\varphi(0),
\]
so
\[
\langle u'',\varphi\rangle
=
\langle2\delta_0,\varphi\rangle.
\]
Since this holds for every
\[
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R),
\]
we conclude that
\[
\boxed{
\frac{d^2}{dx^2}|x|
=
2\delta_0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R).
}
\]

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 3
text:
Remark
Classically,
\[
u'(x)
=
\begin{cases}
-1, & x<0,\\
1, & x>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus, in the sense of distributions,
\[
u'
=
\operatorname{sgn}(x).
\]
The function \(\operatorname{sgn}(x)\) has a jump of size
\[
1-(-1)=2
\]
at the origin. Its distributional derivative is therefore
\[
(\operatorname{sgn}x)'
=
2\delta_0.
\]
Hence one may also summarize the calculation as
\[
|x|'
=
\operatorname{sgn}(x),
\qquad
|x|''
=
2\delta_0.
\]
This is a basic example showing that distributional differentiation detects jump discontinuities through Dirac masses.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 2
text:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and let
\[
f\in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega).
\]
Define
\[
T_f(\varphi)
=
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).
\]
Prove that \(T_f\) is a distribution on \(\Omega\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 2
text:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and let
\[
f\in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega).
\]
Define
\[
T_f(\varphi)
=
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).
\]
Prove that \(T_f\) is a distribution on \(\Omega\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 2
text:
Solution
Recall that a distribution on \(\Omega\) is a continuous linear functional on
\[
\mathcal D(\Omega)
=
C_c^\infty(\Omega).
\]
We show that \(T_f\) is well-defined, linear, and continuous.

Well-definedness
Let
\[
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).
\]
Since \(\varphi\) has compact support, there exists a compact set
\[
K\subset\Omega
\]
such that
\[
\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset K.
\]
Because
\[
f\in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega),
\]
we have
\[
\int_K|f(x)|\,dx<\infty.
\]
Moreover, \(\varphi\) is bounded on \(K\). Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_\Omega |f(x)\varphi(x)|\,dx
&=
\int_K |f(x)\varphi(x)|\,dx\\
&\leq
\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(K)}
\int_K|f(x)|\,dx\\
&<\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \(T_f(\varphi)\) is well-defined.


Linearity
Let \(\varphi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)\) and let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_f(a\varphi+b\psi)
&=
\int_\Omega
f(x)\bigl(a\varphi(x)+b\psi(x)\bigr)\,dx\\
&=
aT_f(\varphi)+bT_f(\psi).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(T_f\) is linear.


Continuity
Let
\[
\varphi_j\to0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D(\Omega).
\]
By the definition of convergence in \(\mathcal D(\Omega)\), there exists a compact set
\[
K\subset\Omega
\]
such that
\[
\operatorname{supp}\varphi_j\subset K
\]
for all sufficiently large \(j\), and
\[
\sup_{x\in K}
|D^\alpha\varphi_j(x)|
\to0
\]
for every multi-index \(\alpha\).
In particular, taking \(\alpha=0\),
\[
\|\varphi_j\|_{L^\infty(K)}
\to0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|T_f(\varphi_j)|
&=
\left|
\int_K f(x)\varphi_j(x)\,dx
\right|\\
&\leq
\int_K|f(x)||\varphi_j(x)|\,dx\\
&\leq
\|f\|_{L^1(K)}
\|\varphi_j\|_{L^\infty(K)}\\
&\to0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
T_f(\varphi_j)\to0.
\]
Hence \(T_f\) is continuous on \(\mathcal D(\Omega)\).
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
T_f\in\mathcal D'(\Omega).
}
\]
Thus every locally integrable function defines a distribution.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 4, Problem 2
text:
Remark
A distribution induced by a locally integrable function is called a regular distribution.
We usually identify \(f\) with its associated distribution and simply write
\[
\langle f,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.
\]
This identification is injective: if
\[
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=0
\]
for every \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)\), then
\[
f=0
\]
almost everywhere in \(\Omega\).
Thus
\[
L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega)
\hookrightarrow
\mathcal D'(\Omega).
\]

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 1, Problem 1
text:
Let \(B(0,1)\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be the unit ball. Determine for which \(s\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\int_{B(0,1)} \frac{1}{\lvert x\rvert^s}\,dx < +\infty.
\]

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 1, Problem 1
text:
Let \(B(0,1)\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be the unit ball. Determine for which \(s\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\int_{B(0,1)} \frac{1}{\lvert x\rvert^s}\,dx < +\infty.
\]

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 1, Problem 1
text:
Solution
The only possible singularity of the integrand is at the origin. Using polar coordinates,
\[
x=r\omega,\qquad r\in(0,1),\quad \omega\in S^{n-1},
\]
and
\[
dx=r^{n-1}\,dr\,d\omega.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\int_{B(0,1)} \frac{1}{\lvert x\rvert^s}\,dx
=
\int_{S^{n-1}}\int_0^1 r^{-s}r^{n-1}\,dr\,d\omega
=
\lvert S^{n-1}\rvert\int_0^1 r^{n-1-s}\,dr.
\]
Recall that
\[
\int_0^1 r^\alpha\,dr<+\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\alpha>-1.
\]
Hence the integral is finite if and only if
\[
n-1-s>-1,
\]
that is,
\[
\boxed{s<n}.
\]
More precisely, when \(s<n\),
\[
\int_{B(0,1)} \frac{1}{\lvert x\rvert^s}\,dx
=
\frac{\lvert S^{n-1}\rvert}{n-s}.
\]
When \(s=n\), the radial integral becomes
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{dr}{r},
\]
which diverges logarithmically; when \(s>n\), it diverges even more strongly.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 1, Problem 1
text:
Remark
This is a basic example of the general principle that, in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), a point singularity of order \(\lvert x\rvert^{-s}\) is locally integrable near the origin exactly when \(s<n\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 2
text:
Construct a counterexample showing that the continuous embedding
\[
C^1(\overline{\Omega})
\hookrightarrow
C^{0,1}(\overline{\Omega})
\]
is not compact, even when \(\Omega\) is a bounded convex domain.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 2
text:
Construct a counterexample showing that the continuous embedding
\[
C^1(\overline{\Omega})
\hookrightarrow
C^{0,1}(\overline{\Omega})
\]
is not compact, even when \(\Omega\) is a bounded convex domain.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 2
text:
Solution
It is enough to consider the one-dimensional convex domain
\[
\Omega=(0,1).
\]
For \(k\geq1\), define
\[
u_k(x)
=
\frac{1}{\pi 2^k}
\sin(\pi 2^k x),
\qquad
x\in[0,1].
\]
Then
\[
u_k'(x)
=
\cos(\pi 2^k x).
\]
Hence
\[
\|u_k\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}
\leq
\frac{1}{\pi2^k}
\leq
\frac1\pi,
\]
and
\[
\|u_k'\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}
=
1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\|u_k\|_{C^1([0,1])}
=
\|u_k\|_{L^\infty}
+
\|u_k'\|_{L^\infty}
\leq
1+\frac1\pi.
\]
Thus \(\{u_k\}\) is bounded in \(C^1([0,1])\).
We now show that it has no convergent subsequence in \(C^{0,1}([0,1])\).
Recall that for a continuously differentiable function \(v\) on \([0,1]\),
\[
[v]_{C^{0,1}}
=
\sup_{x\neq y}
\frac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|}
=
\|v'\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}.
\]
Let \(l>k\). Consider the point
\[
x_k=2^{-k}.
\]
Then
\[
u_k'(x_k)
=
\cos(\pi)
=
-1.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
u_l'(x_k)
=
\cos\left(\pi2^l2^{-k}\right)
=
\cos\left(\pi2^{l-k}\right).
\]
Since \(l-k\geq1\), the integer \(2^{l-k}\) is even, and hence
\[
u_l'(x_k)=1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
|u_l'(x_k)-u_k'(x_k)|
=
2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\|u_l'-u_k'\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}
\geq2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
[u_l-u_k]_{C^{0,1}}
=
\|u_l'-u_k'\|_{L^\infty}
\geq2.
\]
Thus
\[
\|u_l-u_k\|_{C^{0,1}([0,1])}
\geq2
\]
whenever \(l>k\).
Hence \(\{u_k\}\) has no Cauchy subsequence in \(C^{0,1}([0,1])\), and therefore it has no convergent subsequence in \(C^{0,1}([0,1])\).
We conclude that
\[
\boxed{
C^1([0,1])
\hookrightarrow
C^{0,1}([0,1])
\text{ is not compact}.
}
\]
Thus, even for a bounded convex domain,
\[
\boxed{
C^1(\overline{\Omega})
\hookrightarrow
C^{0,1}(\overline{\Omega})
}
\]
is in general not a compact embedding.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 3, Problem 2
text:
Remark
Notice that in this example,
\[
\|u_k\|_{L^\infty}\to0,
\]
so
\[
u_k\to0
\]
uniformly.
The obstruction to compactness comes entirely from the first derivatives:
\[
u_k'(x)
=
\cos(\pi2^k x),
\]
which oscillate more and more rapidly while retaining the same \(L^\infty\) norm.
This illustrates the distinction between the compact embedding
\[
C^1(\overline{\Omega})
\hookrightarrow
C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{\Omega}),
\qquad
0\leq\alpha<1,
\]
and the borderline embedding into \(C^{0,1}\), which is not compact.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 2, Problem 1
text:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and suppose that
\[
u_k\rightharpoonup u
\quad\text{weakly in }X
\]
and
\[
\|u_k\|_X\to \|u\|_X.
\]
Does it follow that
\[
u_k\to u
\quad\text{strongly in }X?
\]
In particular, what happens when \(X=L^p(\Omega)\) for \(1\leq p\leq\infty\)?

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 2, Problem 1
text:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and suppose that
\[
u_k\rightharpoonup u
\quad\text{weakly in }X
\]
and
\[
\|u_k\|_X\to \|u\|_X.
\]
Does it follow that
\[
u_k\to u
\quad\text{strongly in }X?
\]
In particular, what happens when \(X=L^p(\Omega)\) for \(1\leq p\leq\infty\)?

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 2, Problem 1
text:
Solution
In a general Banach space, the conclusion is false.
For \(L^p(\Omega)\), the situation is as follows:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
1<p<\infty &: \quad \text{the implication is true},\\
p=1 &: \quad \text{the implication is false in general},\\
p=\infty &: \quad \text{the implication is false in general}.
\end{aligned}}
\]
The positive result for \(1<p<\infty\) follows from the uniform convexity of \(L^p\).

The case \(1<p<\infty\)
For every \(1<p<\infty\), the space \(L^p(\Omega)\) is uniformly convex. We prove more generally that in every uniformly convex Banach space,
\[
u_k\rightharpoonup u,
\qquad
\|u_k\|_X\to\|u\|_X
\]
imply
\[
u_k\to u
\quad\text{strongly in }X.
\]
If \(u=0\), then
\[
\|u_k-u\|_X=\|u_k\|_X\to0,
\]
so the conclusion is immediate.
Suppose now that \(\|u\|_X>0\). Define
\[
v_k=\frac{u_k}{\|u_k\|_X},
\qquad
v=\frac{u}{\|u\|_X}.
\]
Since
\[
\|u_k\|_X\to\|u\|_X>0,
\]
we have
\[
v_k\rightharpoonup v,
\]
and
\[
\|v_k\|_X=\|v\|_X=1.
\]
Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(v_k\) does not converge strongly to \(v\). Passing to a subsequence if necessary, there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
\|v_k-v\|_X\geq\varepsilon
\]
for every \(k\).
By uniform convexity, there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\left\|
\frac{v_k+v}{2}
\right\|_X
\leq 1-\delta.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\frac{v_k+v}{2}\rightharpoonup v.
\]
Since the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous,
\[
\|v\|_X
\leq
\liminf_{k\to\infty}
\left\|
\frac{v_k+v}{2}
\right\|_X.
\]
Therefore,
\[
1
\leq
\liminf_{k\to\infty}
\left\|
\frac{v_k+v}{2}
\right\|_X
\leq
1-\delta,
\]
which is impossible.
Hence
\[
v_k\to v
\quad\text{strongly in }X.
\]
Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|u_k-u\|_X
&=
\left\|
\|u_k\|_Xv_k-\|u\|_Xv
\right\|_X\\
&\leq
\|u_k\|_X\|v_k-v\|_X
+
\left|
\|u_k\|_X-\|u\|_X
\right|.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both terms tend to zero. Thus
\[
u_k\to u
\quad\text{strongly in }X.
\]
Since \(L^p(\Omega)\) is uniformly convex whenever \(1<p<\infty\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{
u_k\rightharpoonup u
\text{ in }L^p,
\quad
\|u_k\|_{L^p}\to\|u\|_{L^p}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
u_k\to u
\text{ in }L^p
}
\]
for every \(1<p<\infty\).


The case \(p=1\)
The conclusion fails in \(L^1\).
Let \(r_k\) be the \(k\)-th Rademacher function on \((0,1)\). Thus \(r_k\) takes only the values \(1\) and \(-1\), with increasingly rapid dyadic oscillations.
We first observe that
\[
r_k\rightharpoonup0
\quad\text{weakly in }L^1(0,1).
\]
Indeed, let \(\varphi\in L^\infty(0,1)\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose a dyadic step function \(h\) such that
\[
\|\varphi-h\|_{L^1}<\varepsilon.
\]
For sufficiently large \(k\), the function \(r_k\) has zero average on each dyadic interval on which \(h\) is constant. Hence
\[
\int_0^1 h r_k\,dx=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|
\int_0^1\varphi r_k\,dx
\right|
&=
\left|
\int_0^1(\varphi-h)r_k\,dx
\right|\\
&\leq
\|\varphi-h\|_{L^1}
<\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
r_k\rightharpoonup0
\quad\text{in }L^1(0,1).
\]
Now define
\[
u_k=1+r_k,
\qquad
u=1.
\]
Then
\[
u_k\rightharpoonup u
\quad\text{in }L^1(0,1).
\]
Moreover, \(u_k\) takes the values \(0\) and \(2\), each on a set of measure \(1/2\), so
\[
\|u_k\|_{L^1}=1=\|u\|_{L^1}.
\]
However,
\[
\|u_k-u\|_{L^1}
=
\|r_k\|_{L^1}
=
1
\]
for every \(k\).
Hence
\[
u_k\not\to u
\quad\text{strongly in }L^1(0,1).
\]
Therefore the implication fails for \(p=1\).


The case \(p=\infty\)
The conclusion also fails for \(p=\infty\).
Consider
\[
\ell^\infty
=
L^\infty(\mathbb N),
\]
where \(\mathbb N\) is equipped with counting measure. Let \(e_k\) denote the \(k\)-th standard basis vector,
\[
e_k=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots).
\]
We first claim that
\[
e_k\rightharpoonup0
\quad\text{weakly in }\ell^\infty.
\]
Let
\[
\Phi\in(\ell^\infty)^*,
\]
and set
\[
a_k=\Phi(e_k).
\]
For every finite set \(F\subset\mathbb N\), choose scalars \(\varepsilon_k\) with
\[
|\varepsilon_k|=1
\]
such that
\[
\varepsilon_k a_k=|a_k|.
\]
Then
\[
\left\|
\sum_{k\in F}\varepsilon_k e_k
\right\|_{\ell^\infty}
=1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k\in F}|a_k|
&=
\Phi\left(
\sum_{k\in F}\varepsilon_k e_k
\right)\\
&\leq
\|\Phi\|.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\Phi(e_k)|<\infty.
\]
In particular,
\[
\Phi(e_k)\to0.
\]
Since this holds for every \(\Phi\in(\ell^\infty)^*\),
\[
e_k\rightharpoonup0
\quad\text{in }\ell^\infty.
\]
Now let
\[
u=(1,1,1,\ldots)
\]
and define
\[
u_k=u-2e_k.
\]
Since \(e_k\rightharpoonup0\),
\[
u_k\rightharpoonup u
\quad\text{weakly in }\ell^\infty.
\]
Every coordinate of \(u_k\) is equal to \(1\), except for the \(k\)-th coordinate, which is \(-1\). Therefore,
\[
\|u_k\|_{\ell^\infty}
=
1
=
\|u\|_{\ell^\infty}.
\]
Thus the norms converge. However,
\[
\|u_k-u\|_{\ell^\infty}
=
\|-2e_k\|_{\ell^\infty}
=
2
\]
for every \(k\).
Consequently,
\[
u_k\not\to u
\quad\text{strongly in }\ell^\infty.
\]
Hence the implication fails for \(p=\infty\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 2, Problem 1
text:
Remark
The property
\[
u_k\rightharpoonup u,
\qquad
\|u_k\|\to\|u\|
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
u_k\to u
\]
is known as the Radon–Riesz property, or the Kadec–Klee property.
Every uniformly convex Banach space has this property. In particular,
\[
\boxed{
L^p(\Omega)\text{ has this property for }1<p<\infty.
}
\]
In contrast, \(L^1\) and \(L^\infty\) do not have this property in general.
The Hilbert space case \(p=2\) is especially simple. Indeed,
\[
\|u_k-u\|_{L^2}^2
=
\|u_k\|_{L^2}^2
+
\|u\|_{L^2}^2
-
2\langle u_k,u\rangle.
\]
Weak convergence gives
\[
\langle u_k,u\rangle
\to
\|u\|_{L^2}^2,
\]
while convergence of the norms gives
\[
\|u_k\|_{L^2}^2
\to
\|u\|_{L^2}^2.
\]
Hence
\[
\|u_k-u\|_{L^2}\to0.
\]
One should also distinguish weak convergence from weak-* convergence in \(L^\infty\). Weak-* convergence is tested against the chosen predual, whereas weak convergence is tested against the entire dual \((L^\infty)^*\). The counterexample above uses genuine weak convergence in \(\ell^\infty\).

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 1, Problem 2
text: Give an example of a Hilbert space which is not separable.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 1, Problem 2
text: Give an example of a Hilbert space which is not separable.

title: Sobolev Spaces — Week 1, Problem 2
text:
Solution
Consider the Hilbert space
\[
\ell^2(\mathbb R)
=
\left\{
x=(x_i)_{i\in\mathbb R}:
\sum_{i\in\mathbb R}|x_i|^2<\infty
\right\},
\]
equipped with the inner product
\[
\langle x,y\rangle
=
\sum_{i\in\mathbb R}x_i\overline{y_i}.
\]
It is a standard fact that \(\ell^2(\mathbb R)\) is a Hilbert space. We show that it is not separable.
For each \(i\in\mathbb R\), define \(e_i\in\ell^2(\mathbb R)\) by
\[
e_i(j)=\delta_{ij}.
\]
Then
\[
\{e_i:i\in\mathbb R\}
\]
is an uncountable orthonormal family. In particular, for any \(i\neq j\),
\[
\|e_i-e_j\|=\sqrt{2}.
\]
Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\ell^2(\mathbb R)\) is separable. Then there exists a countable dense subset \(D\subset\ell^2(\mathbb R)\).
For each \(i\in\mathbb R\), by the density of \(D\), choose \(d_i\in D\) such that
\[
\|e_i-d_i\|<\frac12.
\]
We claim that the points \(d_i\) are all distinct. Indeed, if \(d_i=d_j=d\) for some \(i\neq j\), then by the triangle inequality,
\[
\|e_i-e_j\|
\le
\|e_i-d\|+\|d-e_j\|
<1,
\]
which contradicts
\[
\|e_i-e_j\|=\sqrt{2}.
\]
Therefore the map
\[
i\longmapsto d_i
\]
is injective from \(\mathbb R\) into \(D\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{card}(D)
\ge
\operatorname{card}(\mathbb R),
\]
so \(D\) is uncountable, contradicting our assumption.
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\ell^2(\mathbb R)\text{ is a nonseparable Hilbert space}.}
\]
